strengths: The core idea—using a (branched) double-cover map to lift interval-valued color attributes (saturation, luminance) onto a circle so that a genuine cyclic group structure and exact group convolution can be built—is a creative and original extension of the color-equivariance line of work (Lengyel et al. 2023; Yang et al. 2024), combining ideas from topology (covering spaces) with equivariant network design in a way not previously explored for color.

The paper provides formal definitions of the hue/saturation/luminance groups and group actions, and includes appendix proofs that the discretized groups satisfy the group axioms, adding a degree of rigor to the construction.

Experiments span a reasonably broad set of settings: synthetic controlled datasets (3D Shapes, hue/saturation/luminance/HSL shift), a lighting-shift benchmark (small NORB), several natural-image classification benchmarks under saturation/luminance shift (Caltech-101, CIFAR-10/100, Stanford Cars, Oxford Pets, STL-10), and a real-world medical imaging dataset with natural color imbalance (Camelyon17).

The paper includes thoughtful diagnostic analyses beyond raw accuracy: quantitative equivariance error, lifting round-trip error, and an entropy/coverage-based analysis of the lifting layer that is used to motivate a principled group-order selection heuristic.

The limitations section candidly acknowledges the computational overhead typical of GCNNs, and the "degenerate lifting" discussion is a genuinely honest disclosure of a real weakness in the proposed construction rather than an attempt to hide it.
weaknesses: The central mathematical device, π(θ) = (c/2) sin θ, is not a topological covering map in the strict sense claimed throughout the paper (a covering map must be a local homeomorphism everywhere), since sin has critical/branch points at θ = π/2, 3π/2 where the map fails to be locally injective; this is implicitly confirmed by the paper's own "degenerate lifting" section, which describes exactly this failure mode. The repeated claim of "perfect equivariance" is therefore somewhat overstated: equivariance holds trivially once inputs are already represented on the discretized cyclic group, but the lift from real interval-valued saturation/luminance values to that group is provably lossy/non-faithful at and near branch points, which is a substantive caveat that is not clearly foregrounded when the title and abstract assert "perfect" equivariance.

The group action equations for saturation/luminance (e.g., Eq. 8, φ_s(s_i, x) = (x_h, π((x_s + s_i) mod 2π), x_l)) appear to add an interval-valued pixel quantity x_s directly to an angle-valued group element s_i before applying mod 2π and π, which is dimensionally inconsistent unless x_s is silently assumed to already be an angle; this notational imprecision makes it difficult to verify that the claimed equivariance proofs and downstream implementation are actually self-consistent.

Several textual claims are not well supported by the reported tables. For example, Section 5.2 states that "the generalization performance of T³CEN consistently exceeds that of baseline models" on the color-shift-in-the-wild experiments, but Table 5 shows multiple cases where ResNet-aug or LCER variants outperform all T³CEN configurations (e.g., CIFAR-100 and Stanford Cars under saturation shift), which is an overclaim relative to the presented evidence.

Many of the headline comparisons (e.g., Table 1 hue-shift results, in-distribution A/A splits throughout) show near-identical 0.00 error for both LCER and T³CEN, indicating these particular tasks are saturated and not informative for discriminating between the two equivariant methods; the paper leans on these ties as evidence of "on par or better" performance without discussing this saturation.

The proposed extensions to RGB-shift equivariance and scale equivariance are only demonstrated qualitatively (a single commutativity figure each) with no quantitative classification results, no dataset/task description for the scale experiment, and an equation (Eq. 24) that appears to contain an unexplained/undefined variable (g_i) and does not clearly correspond to a meaningful notion of image rescaling; these sections read as preliminary additions that do not meet the same evidentiary bar as the main HSL contribution.

Despite explicitly listing computational expense as the primary limitation, no wall-clock training/inference time or FLOPs comparisons are provided against the baselines, making it impossible for readers to gauge the practical cost-benefit tradeoff of the proposed method.

Results on the real-world Camelyon17 dataset are mixed and exhibit high variance across seeds (e.g., ±5-9 points of error), with several T³CEN configurations (e.g., H4S4L4, S4L4) not clearly outperforming the strongest LCER variant, weakening the claim of consistent robustness improvement on realistic color-imbalanced data.

The "selecting the right order" entropy-density heuristic, while an interesting practical tool, is introduced somewhat post hoc and is only validated on a single small-scale MNIST hue-shift experiment, limiting confidence in its general applicability.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated problem: existing color-equivariant CNNs (e.g., LCER) approximate saturation/luminance shifts with a clipped translation group, which is known to introduce boundary artifacts.

The idea of using a smooth interval-to-circle lifting instead of a clipped translation is a reasonable engineering fix that could reduce boundary artifacts and improve gradient behavior near saturation/luminance extremes.

The empirical evaluation is broad, spanning synthetic (3D Shapes, hue/saturation/luminance/HSL shifted variants, hue-shifted MNIST), medical (Camelyon17), and natural image benchmarks (Caltech-101, CIFAR-10/100, Stanford Cars, Oxford Pets, STL-10), with several random seeds and reported standard deviations.
Quantitative equivariance-error and lifting-error analyses (Figs. 3, 4, 9) attempt to directly substantiate the central claim, going beyond purely qualitative feature-map visualizations.
Additional extensions (RGB channels, scale) are presented to argue the lifting idea is more broadly applicable, which if sound would increase the significance of the contribution.
weaknesses: Central mathematical claim appears technically flawed: the paper defines its 'covering map' as π(θ) = (c/2) sin θ from T¹ to the interval, but sin restricted to a circle is not an honest covering map in the standard sense used in the Background section (smooth, surjective, satisfying local 'evenness')—it has critical/branch points at θ = ±π/2 where the map is only 1-to-1 rather than 2-to-1, violating the evenly-covered condition the authors themselves state is required. This is acknowledged implicitly in Section 5.4 ('Degenerate lifting'), which describes exactly this failure mode, yet the paper still calls the construction a 'double-cover' and builds the entire theoretical narrative and title ('Perfect Color Equivariance', 'truly equivariant') on this claim without rigorously verifying or even discussing the branching/degeneracy issue in the main text where the map is introduced.

The redefinition of what a 'saturation/luminance shift' means (a rotation on the lifted circle rather than a genuine interval translation) is not clearly reconciled with what is tested as 'saturation shift' in the OOD experiments (Appendix D.2 describes shifts as fixed interval increments). It is unclear whether the network's formal equivariance guarantee (to circle-group shifts) actually corresponds to the physical/perceptual transformations used to construct the shifted test sets, so the near-zero equivariance error in Fig. 3/9 may be a somewhat tautological consequence of testing the model against its own (possibly non-physical) redefinition of the transformation rather than a meaningful measure of real-world robustness.

The core technical contribution over LCER (Yang et al., 2024) is narrow: essentially replacing a clipped-translation lifting with a sin-based lifting for two of three HSL channels, while the hue-channel treatment and overall convolutional architecture are unchanged from prior work. This is an incremental modification rather than a substantially new architectural or theoretical idea.

Presentation is uneven, with number of typos and internal inconsistencies (e.g., Eq. 24 in the scale-equivariance application mixes 'g_i' and 'α_i', 'hypertorodoidal' vs 'hypertoroidal', 'at with', 'the models are convolved with is'), suggesting insufficient proofreading, which reduces confidence in the correctness of other unchecked derivations (e.g., the lengthy but somewhat redundant group-axiom proofs in Appendix B, which are largely mechanical restatements of the cyclic-group case already known to hold).

Some quantitative results appear self-serving or under-explained: e.g., in Table 6 (Camelyon17) T³CEN-S4 wins by a large margin while T³CEN-H4S4L4 (the fully equivariant, headline configuration) performs worse than several partial configurations, undercutting the narrative that full HSL equivariance is uniformly beneficial; the paper attributes this to filter-count trade-offs but does not control for this confound rigorously (e.g., no ablation holding capacity truly fixed while varying only group order in a principled way beyond the anecdotal MNIST experiment in Appendix C.1).

The scale-equivariance and RGB-equivariance extensions (Section 5, end) are presented only qualitatively via single feature-map visualizations (Fig. 7) with no quantitative equivariance error or downstream task evaluation, making these claims of generality anecdotal rather than substantiated.

No wall-clock/memory comparison is given despite the Limitations section explicitly acknowledging increased computational cost relative to conventional CNNs; the magnitude of this overhead is never quantified, making it hard to judge the practical trade-off.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and concrete limitation of prior color-equivariant work (Yang et al. 2024/LCER): saturation and luminance are bounded intervals, so modeling them as translation groups requires clipping/zero-padding that breaks equivariance. The paper's diagnosis of this problem is clear and well illustrated (Figures 2-4).

The core idea—lifting an interval-valued quantity to a circle via a double-cover so that a genuine group convolution can be applied—is a reasonable and potentially useful technical contribution, and the group axioms (associativity, identity, inverse) are verified explicitly in the appendix for hue/saturation/luminance groups.

Extensive empirical evaluation across many settings: synthetic single/multi-channel shift benchmarks (3D Shapes, small NORB, hue-shift MNIST), a real medical-imaging robustness benchmark (Camelyon17), and several natural-image classification datasets (Caltech-101, CIFAR-10/100, Stanford Cars, Oxford Pets, STL-10) under saturation/luminance shift.

Quantitative equivariance-error and lifting-error comparisons against LCER (Figures 3, 4, 9) convincingly show that the proposed cyclic construction is numerically far closer to exact equivariance than the translation-based baseline.

The entropy-based analysis of lifting coverage (Section 5.4) is a nice diagnostic tool that gives a principled, data-dependent heuristic for choosing group order, and is validated empirically on hue-shift MNIST (Figure 8).
weaknesses: The central mathematical construction is called a 'covering map' / 'double-cover' (analogized to the S^3→SO(3) double cover), but the map π(θ) = (c/2) sin θ used for saturation/luminance has fold (branch) points where it fails to be a local homeomorphism — this contradicts the paper's own definition of a covering map in Section 3 ('smooth, surjective, and satisfies evenness'). The 'degenerate lifting' phenomenon described in Section 5.4 is precisely a symptom of this branching, so the terminology is technically inconsistent with the paper's own stated definitions and with the S^3/SO(3) analogy (which has no branch points).

The notation for the group action on saturation/luminance (e.g., Eq. 8, Eq. 28) mixes raw interval-valued channel values (x_s in [0,c]) with angular group elements (s_i, mod 2π) without clarifying how/where the interval value is converted to an angle before the addition; this type ambiguity makes the construction hard to verify or reproduce precisely from the text alone.

The 'Application to scale equivariance' section (Eq. 24) appears to contain an error: it defines the action on pixel coordinates using an undefined variable g_i (rather than α_i) and, more importantly, the operation described (adding a constant to pixel coordinates modulo 2π) implements a translation-like shift of coordinates rather than a multiplicative rescaling, so it is unclear the construction actually captures scale (resolution) equivariance as claimed. This section and the RGB-equivariance extension are supported only by single qualitative examples (Figure 7) with no quantitative equivariance error or downstream task evaluation, making these claimed generalizations of the method under-supported.

Claims of the method 'consistently exceeding' baselines are not fully borne out by the reported tables: in Table 5 (color shift in the wild), ResNet-aug or LCER variants sometimes outperform all T3CEN variants (e.g., CIFAR-100 and Stanford Cars under saturation shift, CIFAR-10 under luminance shift), and in Table 6 (Camelyon17) several T3CEN configurations (H4S4L4, S4L4) underperform LCER-S3/LCER-H4S3. The best-performing T3CEN configuration differs across datasets/tables, which resembles selective reporting rather than a uniformly superior architecture.
No mention of code or model release, which combined with the notational ambiguities above raises reproducibility concerns despite the detailed hyperparameter appendix.

The appendix devotes substantial space to elementary, mechanical proofs that C_N, C_M, C_R are groups under modular addition (Appendix B), which is standard and could be stated in one line by citing that (Z/nZ, +) is a well-known cyclic group, rather than several pages of repetitive modular-arithmetic manipulation; this reduces the effective information density of the appendix.

The paper does not discuss the added computational/implementation cost or accuracy trade-off from the branch/degenerate points in more depth (e.g., how much task-relevant saturation/luminance information is systematically lost near degenerate inputs in real datasets, beyond the synthetic MNIST order-selection experiment), leaving the practical severity of this limitation somewhat unclear.

strengths: The core idea—using a covering-type map to lift bounded, interval-valued color attributes (saturation, luminance) onto a circle so that they admit genuine group (cyclic) structure—is a reasonable and creative way to address the clipping artifacts that arise when saturation/luminance are modeled as translation groups in prior work (LCER/Yang et al. 2024).

The empirical evaluation is broad, spanning synthetic controlled datasets (3D Shapes, hue/saturation/luminance/HSL shifted variants), small NORB (luminance), a real medical imaging benchmark (Camelyon17), several natural-image classification datasets (Caltech-101, CIFAR-10/100, Stanford Cars, Oxford Pets, STL-10) under saturation/luminance shift, and a color-informative task (KUTomaData) to probe failure modes.

Section 5.5 ('Limitation of Color Equivariance') is a notably honest and useful addition: the authors explicitly identify and quantify two settings (color-as-signal, no distribution shift) where the proposed inductive bias hurts performance, which is more rigorous limitations treatment than typical in method papers.

Formal verification that the discretized hue/saturation/luminance sets with modular addition satisfy the group axioms is provided in the appendix, and quantitative analyses of lifting coverage, entropy, and redundant representations give a principled way to choose group order.

The reported reduction in equivariance error and lifting error versus LCER, and consistent (though not uniform) accuracy improvements across most classification benchmarks, provide reasonable evidence that the proposed lifting reduces the artifacts the paper targets.
weaknesses: The paper's central theoretical claim of 'perfect' equivariance is never formally proven for the HSL group convolution/lifting layer itself; the manuscript only proves that the discretized hue/saturation/luminance sets satisfy group axioms and then simply asserts ('It can be shown that...') that the group convolution is equivariant, without a proof or even a proof sketch in the main text or appendix. For a paper whose main selling point is exact equivariance, this is a significant gap.

The use of the term 'covering map' for π(θ) = (c/2) sin θ is imprecise: this map has critical points at θ = ±π/2 (where dπ/dθ = 0), which correspond exactly to the interval endpoints, so it is a branched/folded double cover rather than an honest covering map in the standard topological sense (local homeomorphism everywhere). This subtlety is not discussed, even though it is directly responsible for the 'redundant representations' phenomenon the authors later report empirically (Section 5.4), suggesting the issue is real but under-analyzed rather than merely a minor discretization artifact.

It is unclear that the sinusoidal cyclic action on saturation/luminance corresponds to any physically or perceptually meaningful transformation encountered in real imaging pipelines (e.g., gain/exposure changes, staining variation), unlike the translation-with-clipping model it replaces, which at least approximates common photometric operations. The equivariance-error comparisons (Section 5.1) may therefore be somewhat tautological: T³CEN is compared on an action that matches its own construction by design, while LCER is evaluated against an action it was not designed to represent exactly, making the several-orders-of-magnitude gap less informative about practical benefit than it first appears.

Because parameter count is held fixed by reducing filter depth as HSL order grows, there is a confound between the benefit attributed to equivariance structure and the cost/benefit of reduced network capacity. The paper acknowledges this (e.g., T³CEN-S4 outperforming T³CEN-H4S4 in Table 5) but does not fully disentangle it, leaving some accuracy gains and losses difficult to attribute cleanly to the proposed mechanism.

Results across the large number of T³CEN configurations in Tables 5 and 6 are inconsistent: no single configuration dominates across datasets/shift types, and several 'combined' configurations (e.g., H4S4L4) underperform simpler ones (e.g., S4 alone) on Camelyon17, complicating practical takeaways for which configuration to deploy.

The RGB-shift and scale-equivariance extensions in Section 6 are only qualitatively illustrated with single feature-map commutativity figures, with no quantitative equivariance error or downstream task evaluation, making these 'broader applicability' claims largely speculative.

The manuscript has noticeable proofreading issues that reduce confidence in the presentation's care: two consecutive sections are both titled 'Background' (Sections 3 and 4, where Section 4 should presumably be the Method section), the model is referred to as 'T⁴CEN' instead of 'T³CEN' in multiple places in Section 6, the title itself contains a typo ('hypertorodoidal' in the abstract text), and Equation 24 appears to contain a copy-paste variable error (using g_i instead of α_i).

strengths: The paper identifies a real limitation in prior work (Yang et al., 2024): modeling saturation/luminance as interval-clipped translations introduces artifacts, and the proposed double-cover lifting reduces measured equivariance/lifting error by several orders of magnitude (Fig. 3, Fig. 4) relative to LCER.

The hue, saturation, luminance, and joint HSL group actions are formally specified, and Appendix B verifies the group axioms (associativity, identity, inverse) for the cyclic constructions, giving the method a degree of mathematical grounding.

The experimental scope is broad: synthetic 3D Shapes/NORB/MNIST equivariance studies, six 'in-the-wild' classification datasets under saturation/luminance shift, and a real medical-imaging robustness study (Camelyon17), together with augmentation baselines (AugMix, DeepAugment, Planckian Jitter).

Section 5.5 is a candid limitations study (color-as-signal on KUTomaData, no-distribution-shift on hue-MNIST) that honestly documents when the equivariance inductive bias hurts rather than helps, which is a valuable and unusually forthright addition.

Extension of the lifting construction to RGB-space and scale transformations (Section 6) suggests the idea may generalize beyond the HSL setting, which if substantiated would broaden the contribution's significance.
weaknesses: The central 'double-cover' terminology is used loosely: mapping θ↦(c/2)sinθ from the circle to a bounded interval is not a covering map in the standard topological sense (a covering map is a local homeomorphism everywhere and an interval is simply connected, so it cannot have a nontrivial connected covering space). The construction is degenerate exactly at the interval endpoints/midpoint, producing the 'redundant representations' the authors themselves report (Section 5.4, Eq. 19) — this undercuts the 'perfect equivariance' framing and is described as a coverage/entropy nuisance rather than acknowledged as a structural failure of the claimed covering-map formalism.

It is unclear that shifting an angle θ additively corresponds to a physically meaningful saturation/luminance shift in the original interval, since π(θ)=(c/2)sinθ is nonlinear; equal steps in the circle group do not correspond to equal (linear/additive) changes in saturation/luminance as typically applied in image editing or as used for LCER's translation group. This raises the concern that the equivariance guarantee is with respect to a reparametrized, physically non-standard notion of 'shift,' making the equivariance-error comparisons against LCER (Fig. 3, 4) not a like-for-like comparison.

Real-world results are inconsistent with the headline claim: in Camelyon17 (Table 5) the full T3CEN-H4S4L4 model (19.97) is worse than the single-channel T3CEN-S4 (12.11) and even worse than LCER-S3 (16.08); similarly in Table 6 no single HSL configuration wins uniformly across datasets. This suggests the practical benefit is fragile and configuration-dependent, and the paper offers no principled, validated procedure (tested on real data, not just synthetic entropy plots) for choosing the right configuration in advance.

The perfect (0.00/0.00) accuracy reported for T3CEN-H4S4L4 on the synthetic HSL-shifted 3D Shapes dataset (Table 4) is suspicious given that the group order used for training was matched to the discretization used to generate the shifted test set; this risks an experiment that trivially favors the proposed architecture rather than demonstrating generalization to realistic continuous shifts.

Computational cost is substantial and under-discussed: Table 12 shows the full HSL model requires ~32x the memory and runs ~12x slower than the base single-channel model, yet the accuracy gains over simpler configurations (or over LCER) are often marginal (a few points) or even negative (Camelyon17). The Limitations paragraph mentions this only in one generic sentence without quantifying the accuracy/compute trade-off shown in the appendix.

Since hue lifting is explicitly borrowed unchanged from Yang et al. (2024), and T3CEN-H4 numbers are identical to LCER-H4 to two decimal places in multiple tables, the genuinely novel contribution is confined to saturation/luminance handling; framing the whole HSL system as 'perfectly equivariant' somewhat overstates the scope of what is new.

Presentation/proofreading issues undermine confidence in rigor: Section numbering duplicates 'Background' for both Section 3 and Section 4 (the latter should be 'Method'), and the RGB/scale subsections refer to 'T4CEN' instead of 'T3CEN,' suggesting insufficient proofreading of a paper whose core claims rest on precise mathematical definitions.

Considerable space (a full appendix page) is devoted to proving that a discretized cyclic group under modular addition satisfies group axioms — a standard, unsurprising fact — while more critical questions (e.g., justification of the covering-map claim, sensitivity of results to order selection on real data) receive comparatively little space or rigorous treatment.

The 'principled' order-selection method (Section 5.4) is validated only on synthetic hue-shifted MNIST and abstract entropy plots, not shown to transfer to the real datasets (Camelyon17, Caltech-101, etc.) where the paper's own tables show that adding more equivariant channels can hurt performance, so its practical utility is unverified.

strengths: The central idea—lifting bounded interval-valued quantities (saturation, luminance) to a circle via a double-cover (θ ↦ (c/2) sin θ) rather than approximating them with a translation group—is an elegant fix to a genuine limitation of prior work (Yang et al. 2024/LCER), which requires clipping and is thus only approximately equivariant.

The group-theoretic construction is carefully laid out, with explicit definitions of hue/saturation/luminance group actions and appendix proofs that the discretized HSL groups satisfy the group axioms.

Empirical validation is broad: equivariance-error and lifting-error comparisons against LCER, synthetic OOD generalization on 3D Shapes (hue/saturation/HSL) and small NORB (luminance), real-world fine-grained/classification datasets (Caltech-101, CIFAR-10/100, Stanford Cars, Oxford Pets, STL-10), and a real medical imaging benchmark (Camelyon17).

The paper includes an unusually candid limitations study (Section 5.5): it explicitly identifies and quantifies two failure modes of color equivariance (color-as-signal on KUTomaData, and no-distribution-shift capacity cost on hue-shift MNIST), which strengthens the credibility of the overall claims rather than just showcasing favorable results.

The analysis of lifting coverage, redundant representations, and entropy-based order selection (Section 5.4) is a useful and original tool for practically choosing group cardinality, going beyond a pure algorithmic contribution.
Reasonably thorough appendix documentation of datasets, training hyperparameters, and computational cost (memory/throughput vs. LCER), aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The paper asserts 'It can be shown that the HSL group convolution is equivariant to hue, saturation and luminance' but never provides this proof in the main text or appendix; the central claim of 'perfect' equivariance for the full convolutional pipeline is validated only empirically (near-zero measured error attributed to 'computational error'), not established formally, which is a soundness gap given the paper's title and main claim.

Statistical significance is often unclear: many result tables (e.g., Table 6 saturation/luminance-shifted results, Table 5 Camelyon17) report standard deviations that overlap substantially with competing methods, yet the text repeatedly claims T3CEN 'consistently exceeds' or is 'significantly better' without hypothesis testing; only 3 seeds (5 for Camelyon17) are used, which is a thin basis for such strong claims.

The extensions to RGB-shift equivariance and scale equivariance (Section 6) are only demonstrated qualitatively via single feature-map commutativity figures, with no quantitative downstream task results—this weakens the abstract's claim that the lifting 'extends' meaningfully beyond color.

The double-cover map is non-injective (2-to-1 except at extrema), producing 'redundant representations' near certain input values; while honestly documented, this means the practical information capacity of the lifted representation is input-dependent and can be substantially degraded, complicating the 'perfect equivariance' narrative and requiring an extra order-selection heuristic not needed by simpler baselines.

The fixed-parameter-budget protocol (reducing filter depth as group order grows) is acknowledged to sometimes cause higher-order/combined models to underperform lower-order ones (e.g., T3CEN-S4 vs. T3CEN-H4S4 in Table 5), making cross-configuration comparisons and the 'best' configuration to deploy less clear-cut.

There are presentation issues: Section 4 is mislabeled 'Background' (duplicating the title of Section 3) when it is really the Method section; the model is inconsistently referred to as 'T4CEN' in the RGB/scale subsections; no explicit statement of code/data release is provided, which limits full reproducibility despite detailed hyperparameter tables.
